g.text: UART RTS/CTS — one byte of 0xA5 is ten cells, and RTS brackets the whole frame
RTS HIGH — asserted BEFORE CTS is read
CTS HIGH, in response to RTS
ORDER IS ASSERTED, NOT INFERRED. RTS is the MASTER's pin and CTS is the
receiver's; the receiver never drives RTS. A driver that waited for CTS
before asserting RTS deadlocks against a receiver that only raises CTS when
asked, and the TB's second case is exactly what such a receiver looks like.
one cell = 2 TIMER ticks = 520 clks = 8.667 us
RTS released here, and only here
LSB FIRST, and the payload is 0x00, 0xFF, 0xA5
on purpose. 0x00 is eight zero bits behind a
start bit and 0xFF is eight one bits, so a bit
period a little long or a little short shows up
in one of them and not the other; and 0xA5
(1010 0101) is not a bit palindrome, so a
transmitter that shifted the wrong way is
TEN cells: a start bit, eight data bits LSB
first, and a stop bit. The handshake is NOT
a ninth clock — it brackets the frame: RTS is
high from before the first start bit until
after the last stop bit, and it is
re-asserted inside every single OUT, so it
cannot be dropped by a refactor of the bit
